title: Packed prime vector core v1
objective: Implement compiler-owned bit-packed GF(2) vectors and canonical fixed-width small-prime vector kernels with correct dynamic fallbacks, arithmetic, dot products, selectors, differential tests, inspectable native lowering, and focused benchmarks without changing public Vector integration or shared compiler and FFI infrastructure

handoff.summary: The first direct capability probe established that the existing source-transparent UInt64Buffer/NativeRecord compiler cannot express an efficient bit-packed GF(2) vector core. Compiling canonical padding validation stopped at packed_binary_vector.py:32:26 with `unsupported source-transparent operator >>`; inspection of prime-source-ir.cjs confirmed that typed uint64 binary lowering currently admits only +, -, *, %, and //. The required operations &, |, ^, <<, and >> are therefore absent generically. The experimental vector modules were deleted rather than shipping arithmetic emulation or a half-vector abstraction, so this blocked task contains no production change.
risks: Emulating word bit operations with repeated division and remainder would make the storage nominally bit-packed while performing up to 64 scalar iterations per word, defeating the representation's purpose and obscuring a compiler limitation.
Adding vector-specific compiler substitutions would violate source transparency and make the compiler recognize mathematical functions by name.
Finishing only the fixed-width small-GF(p) half would create an incomplete public foundation and weaken the intended shared vector contract.
next_steps: Complete and independently review the separate native-uint64-bitwise-v1 compiler prerequisite, which must implement generic typed uint64 &, |, ^, <<, and >> semantics without changing Python Integer bitwise behavior.
Integrate that prerequisite into the shared baseline, then resume this exact task from the updated base and reintroduce both GF(2) and small-GF(p) modules together.
Retain differential, inspectability, canonical-padding, transactional-output, and focused benchmark requirements when the lane resumes.
